record.paper_title: What Regulates Galaxy Evolution? Open Questions in our Understanding of Galaxy Formation and Evolution.
record.context_brief: Angular momentum and realistic disk-galaxy formation
record.original_question: How can fully cosmological simulations form realistic rotationally supported disk galaxies with thin, high-angular-momentum stellar disks, rather than producing overly compact disks and large bulges through excessive early gas cooling and angular-momentum transfer from baryons to dark matter?

evidence.quote: This produces a net and significant transfer of angular momentum from the baryons to the dark matter, resulting in spiral galaxies with large bulges and compact disks (this is the so called ‘angular momentum catastrophe’).
The formation of a realistic rotationally supported disk galaxy in a fully cosmological simulation is still an open problem.
Despite much progress, however, the formation of thin and high angular momentum stellar disks remains a challenge

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In the standard cold dark matter cosmological framework, baryons are assumed to acquire specific angular momentum comparable to that of their host dark matter halos through tidal torques during the early stages of structure formation. After collapse and dissipation, conservation of angular momentum should allow the baryons to settle into rotationally supported, thin stellar disks with exponential surface-density profiles and small central bulges, in agreement with observed late-type spiral galaxies.

In practice, fully cosmological hydrodynamical simulations that follow gas cooling, star formation, and feedback inside evolving dark matter halos have systematically suffered from the so-called "angular momentum catastrophe": excessive early gas cooling concentrates baryons into dense clumps which, via dynamical friction against the surrounding dark matter, transfer a large fraction of their angular momentum to the halo. The resulting galaxies have disks that are too compact (with radial scale lengths up to an order of magnitude smaller than observed), rotation speeds that are too high, and bulge-to-disk ratios that are too large.

Problem. Devise a prescription within fully cosmological hydrodynamical simulations — specifying the treatment of gas cooling, star formation thresholds, and stellar/AGN feedback (and any required numerical resolution and integration scheme) — under which Milky Way-mass halos at redshift zero host realistic rotationally supported spiral galaxies with thin, high-specific-angular-momentum stellar disks, exponential surface-density profiles with realistic scale lengths, small bulge-to-disk ratios, and flat rotation curves, without artificially transferring angular momentum from the baryons to the dark matter. Establish that the resulting disk population reproduces, statistically, the observed distributions of disk size, specific angular momentum, and morphology across a representative sample of halo masses and merger histories.
artifact.status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made since 2014. Modern cosmological hydrodynamical simulations (e.g., FIRE-2, EAGLE, IllustrisTNG, Auriga) with improved stellar feedback and resolution now routinely produce Milky Way-mass galaxies with realistic thin, rotationally supported stellar disks, largely mitigating the angular momentum catastrophe. However, fully reproducing the observed statistical distributions of disk sizes, specific angular momentum, and bulge-to-disk ratios across galaxy populations remains an active area of research, and detailed angular momentum transfer mechanisms are still being characterized (e.g., 2024 FIRE study). The problem is best classified as partially solved.

status_evidence.title: Angular momentum transfer in cosmological simulations of Milky Way-mass discs
status_evidence.snippet: Examines how accreting gas settles into rotational support in disc outskirts in FIRE-2 simulations, consistent with inside-out disc growth.
status_evidence.claim: Active 2024 research is still characterizing angular-momentum transfer in modern simulations of disk formation.

status_evidence.title: Cosmological Evolution of Galaxies - Shlosman
status_evidence.snippet: Cosmological hydrodynamic simulations with properly tuned star formation and stellar feedback physics are now able to produce galaxies with realistic disk scale lengths, bulge–to–disk ratios and overall angular momentum content.
status_evidence.claim: Modern feedback-regulated simulations largely produce realistic disks, indicating significant progress on the angular momentum catastrophe.

status_evidence.title: Galactic Angular Momentum in Cosmological Zoom-in Simulations
status_evidence.snippet: Zoom-in simulations analyze disk and bulge angular momentum and the galaxy–halo connection.
status_evidence.claim: Recent simulations reproduce key aspects of disk angular momentum content.
